comments.text: There’s not enough room so I’ll keep it short. I visited Lebanon in 1979 during the Lebanese Civil War. My friend lived in the mountains above the city. I passed through 27 checkpoints: Lebanese army, PLO, Shia, Gemayel, Chamoun (the last 2 Maronite Christian militias hated each other!) and Syrian. One taxi brought me from the airport to the green line but refused to go further. I walked on foot to the other side to take a taxi into the mountains. The windows at my friend’s house were shuttered. On no condition was I to open them. Every day the earth shook as Syrian tanks came down. Any cars in the way were smashed and some pushed down the slopes. I peeked through a tiny slit as a tank passed. Five meters away a nervous soldier on a tank with a mounted machine gun, his hand on the trigger pointed in my direction. I visited Dr. Yusuf Hitti, world expert on Arabic science in the Middle Ages. Out of fears for personal safety he stopped lecturing at the American University. My friend took me to Nahr al-Kelb. Imagine my astonishment at seeing the hieroglyphics of Rameses II! I went to Byblos. The sequence was : Semitic alphabet without vowels first used in Phoenician Byblos spread to Phoenician Al-Mina in north Syria, picked up by Greek traders from Euboeia there who took it home, added vowels, changed right-left to left-right, passed it on to Etruscans in Cumae in south Italy who passed it to the Romans (I’m writing this in their alphabet.) We sat on the hillside on a balmy evening listening to intermittent gunfire down in Beirut. I’ll stop here. I’m shocked by the violence visited upon Lebanon by its southern neighbor. The video is absolutely top notch and captures so many facettes and nuances. Grateful for your splendid work.
